title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs
author: Ava Chen
body:
Summary:

This page consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It includes governance, decision-record (ADR) practices, and concrete thresholds we use for production readiness. Use this doc as the primary reference when designing new services or reviewing architecture proposals.

Scope:
- Applies to all customer-facing services (hosted API, dedicated control plane) and internal infrastructure that impacts SLOs.
- Includes guidelines for new service onboarding, code review standards, infra provisioning, model packaging/serving, and monitoring.

Principles (high level):
1. Predictable production behavior: SLOs and operational playbooks are the primary product requirements.
2. Developer ergonomics + safety: Standardized SDKs, clear contracts, and guardrails to prevent regressions.
3. Observable by default: Metrics, logs, and traces shipped with every change.
4. Composable & versioned: APIs and model artifacts must be versioned and backward-compatible where possible.
5. Automate testing and rollout: CI checks, contract tests, canary rollouts, and automatic rollbacks.

Ownership and governance:
- Standards owner: Architecture Working Group (chairs: Ava Chen, Marcus Patel).
- Enforcement: Architecture reviews are required for any service or infra change affecting SLOs or cross-team integrations.
- Exceptions: Documented via ADR and tracked in the architecture backlog.

1) API Standards
- Design principles:
  - RESTful + OpenAPI-first for external endpoints; gRPC or HTTP/2 for high-throughput internal RPCs.
  - Stable, versioned contracts: semantic versioning for public endpoints (v1, v2). Internal contracts may use rolling compatibility checks but require explicit deprecation windows.
  - Idempotency for mutating operations: client-supplied idempotency keys required for any non-retriable side-effecting call.
  - Resource-oriented URLs and consistent pagination (cursor-based).

- Schema & validation:
  - All public APIs must publish an OpenAPI (3.1) spec in the repo and be validated in CI using contract tests.
  - Use JSON Schema for payload validation; prefer explicit fields over open objects.

- Error handling:
  - Use structured error objects: { code, message, details }.
  - Standard HTTP codes: 400 for client, 401/403 for auth, 429 for rate-limit, 5xx for server. 503 with Retry-After for maintenance/failover.

- Rate limiting & quotas:
  - Per-API route rate limits defined in config. Default hosted-api thresholds: burst 300 req/min, sustained 60 req/min per API key. Dedicated customers may override via contract.

- API examples (snippet):
  - OpenAPI path example for /v1/generate documented in the repo with example request/response and streaming guidance.

- Contract testing:
  - Every client-facing SDK must run contract tests in CI against a staging mock for schema and basic functional checks.

2) Coding Standards
- Languages & formatters:
  - Backend services primarily in Go and Python (Go for low-latency runtime services, Python for orchestration and tooling).
  - Formatters: gofmt/golangci-lint for Go; Black + ruff + mypy for Python. Enforce in pre-commit + CI.

- Testing & coverage:
  - Unit tests required for all new logic. Target >= 60% coverage for service packages; critical runtime code (inference stack) must have >= 85% coverage.
  - Integration tests for cross-service interactions; mocked model tests for model-serving code.

- PR process:
  - All PRs require at least one reviewer from the owning team and one reviewer from platform/security if the change touches infra, auth, or networking.
  - PR checklist: design summary, rollback plan, metrics/alerts to create/update, security considerations.

- Dependency management:
  - Pin dependencies, run weekly dependency scans. High/critical CVEs must be addressed within 72 hours for internet-exposed services.

3) Infrastructure Standards
- IaC and provisioning:
  - Terraform modules in the central registry (eng-infra/terraform-and-iac) must be used for cloud resources. No ad-hoc cloud console provisioning for production.
  - Modules must include tagging (team, environment, cost-center), and reuse standard VPC and subnet patterns.

- Networking & security:
  - Default-deny network policies. Use service-to-service mTLS for internal RPCs; mutual TLS or token-based auth for cross-account links.
  - Private-only endpoints for Dedicated/Private control plane by default. Public endpoints must pass threat model review.

- Secrets & keys:
  - Store secrets in KMS-backed vault (HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS integration). CI/CD must not expose secrets in logs.

- Capacity and autoscaling:
  - Autoscaling policies must be defined in Terraform with min/max bounds and target utilization. For GPU-backed pools, min-replicas must be set to prevent cold-starts for latency-critical models.

- Backup and DR:
  - Critical state (customer configs, billing events) must be backed up daily with tested restore runbooks. RPO target: 1 hour for customer-facing control data.

4) Model-Serving Standards
- Packaging & artifacts:
  - Models must be packaged with metadata: model_id, training_commit, quantization_profile, runtime_requirements, input_schema, output_schema, known_limitations. Store artifacts in model registry with immutable versioned URIs.

- Quantization and profiles:
  - Maintain canonical quantization profiles (see confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles). Each profile must include expected latency/quality tradeoffs and unit-cost estimates.

- Runtime compatibility:
  - Runtime config (batching windows, KV cache behavior, max_context) must be declared in the model artifact and validated at deployment. Backwards-incompatible runtime changes require ADR and staged rollout.

- Latency budgets & fallbacks:
  - Per-model latency SLOs documented in the model registry. Example defaults: small LLMs (<=3B): p95 <= 200ms; medium (3B-20B): p95 <= 600ms; large (>20B): p95 <= 1200ms for 128-token requests.
  - Fallback strategy: automatic fallback to a compatible lower-capacity quantized variant when tail latency breach or capacity shortage detected.

- Model versioning and rollouts:
  - Canary policy: start at 1% traffic for 30 minutes with automated quality and latency checks before progressive rollouts (1%, 5%, 25%, 100%).
  - Ability to instant rollback to previous model version with zero-downtime routing change.

- Quality monitoring:
  - Evals integrated into canary: run a predetermined prompt set and compute regressed metrics (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE where applicable, hallucination score). Reject rollouts if regressions exceed thresholds.

5) Observability Standards
- Metrics (prometheus-style):
  - Every service must expose: request_count (counter, labels=route,code), request_duration_seconds (histogram), error_count (counter), in_flight_requests (gauge).
  - Model-serving-specific metrics: tokens_generated, kv_cache_hit_ratio, avg_batch_size, fallback_count.

- Tracing:
  - Use distributed tracing (OTel). Trace every request end-to-end across platform components. Span naming: service.operation[/model].

- Logging:
  - Structured JSON logs with request_id, user_id (anonymized in hosted mode), model_id, route. No PII in logs; redact any user content by default for hosted API.

- Dashboards & SLOs:
  - Standard dashboards (per-route and per-model) created from templated panels. SLOs must be declared in code and config and linked to on-call runbooks.

- Alerts:
  - Alert categories: Sev-1 (SLO burn, data loss, severe errors), Sev-2 (persistent elevated error rate, degradation), Sev-3 (minor regressions).
  - Alert thresholds examples: error_rate > 0.5% for 5 minutes => Sev-2; p95 latency breaches SLO for 15 minutes => Sev-2; SLO error budget burn > 50% in 24h => Sev-1.

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarking
- SLO definitions (example):
  - Hosted Generation API: availability 99.9% monthly; p95 latency per-token (small models) <= 200ms; throughput scaling as configured.
  - Embeddings API: availability 99.95%; p95 latency <= 150ms for 512-dim embeddings.

- Tail-latency and percentiles:
  - Report p50, p90, p95, p99 independently by route and model. Track tail latencies on cold-starts separately.

- Benchmarks and release gating:
  - Every runtime change (kernel, scheduler, quantization) must include a benchmark job that reports regression against historical baselines. Regression threshold: no more than 5% increase in p95 for targeted workloads.
  - Performance release checklist: perf-test results, resource cost delta, regression triage plan.

- Capacity planning:
  - Use historical QPS and sim workloads to project GPU capacity. Maintain burst capacity buffer of 20% for hosted API; dedicated customers have contractual minimums.

7) ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
- Process:
  - Create ADR for any non-trivial design decision affecting architecture, APIs, or infra assumptions. Use the ADR template in this repo.
  - ADR must include: status, context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences, owners, and link to follow-ups.
  - ADR lifecycle: proposed -> accepted -> implemented -> deprecated (if replaced).

- ADR template (example content):
  - Title: Choose short descriptive phrase
  - Date: YYYY-MM-DD
  - Status: proposed | accepted | superseded
  - Context: problem statement and constraints
  - Decision: chosen approach and rationale
  - Consequences: operational impact, migration steps, rollbacks

- Example ADR summary included here:
  - ADR-2025-14: Service Mesh Adoption (accepted 2025-02-11) - Adopted lightweight service mesh for egress controls and identity; excluded from latency-critical inference path to avoid added hop.

8) Release, rollout and rollback procedures
- Canary & progressive rollout pattern:
  1) Deploy canary to 1% traffic for 30 minutes, run automated health checks (latency, error rate, eval prompt-set quality).
  2) If green, expand to 5% for 1 hour and re-check.
  3) Expand to 25% for 2 hours and perform business-metric smoke tests.
  4) Full rollout with final monitoring for 24 hours.

- Rollback triggers:
  - Immediate rollback on any Sev-1 alert, or if canary quality metrics regress beyond pre-defined thresholds.

9) Compliance & Security considerations
- Data residency:
  - Honor customer regional tenancy: Dedicated/Private deployments must keep customer data within declared regions. Documented in deployment manifest.

- PII and logging:
  - Redact PII and user prompt content in hosted logs. Private deployments may configure retention per contract but must document data flows.

Appendix: Key configuration table

| Area | Key config / threshold | Owner | Notes |
|------|-----------------------|-------|-------|
| Hosted API rate limit | burst=300/sustained=60 per API key | eng-platform | Configurable per customer|
| Default model p95 latency | small<=200ms, medium<=600ms, large<=1200ms | eng-serving-runtime | Measured for 128-token requests|
| SLO availability | 99.9% (hosted generation) | eng-sre | Monthly measurement|
| Error alert threshold | error_rate > 0.5% for 5m => Sev-2 | eng-sre | Tunable per route|
| Backup RPO | 1 hour for control-plane data | eng-infra | Nightly restore tests required|

Operational checklists (quick links):

- Model deployment checklist: model artifact, quantization profile, canary prompt set, rollout plan, rollback tested.

FAQ (quick):
Q: When should I create an ADR?
A: Any time a decision affects long-term architecture, APIs, cross-team contracts, or causes non-trivial migration work.

Q: Who sets SLO targets for a new route?
A: Service owners propose SLOs; eng-sre reviews and signs off based on historical data and customer expectations.
